conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in from the ED with abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. I was discharged just a few days ago, and I felt okay that night, but the next morning the pain came back—same as before. It’s in my upper belly, goes to my back, and gets worse after eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds like your typical flare. You mentioned nausea and vomiting too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I haven’t been able to keep anything down. And last night, I threw up and there was a little blood—maybe a tablespoon. It happened again this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. The team noted that—called hematemesis. Given your history of wretching, it’s likely a small tear in the esophagus. Your blood count is stable, so that’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? I was worried it might be something worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can happen with forceful vomiting. You had an EGD three weeks ago, and it showed mild esophagitis but no ulcers or bleeding sites. So we think this is related to the vomiting, not a new bleed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. But why is this pain happening so often now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we’re trying to figure out. You have chronic pancreatitis, which we believe may be linked to your underlying autoimmune issues like Sjogren’s and possible vasculitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’m on methotrexate for that. Shouldn’t that be helping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should, and it has helped with your malabsorption. But your pain flares keep recurring. We’ve consulted rheumatology to see if your vasculitis might be active.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what did they say?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They reviewed your case and don’t think you’re having an active vasculitis flare right now. But we’re waiting on some blood tests—like anti-Ro/La, RNP, and cryoglobulins—to be sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my pancreas? Could this be another pancreatitis attack?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your lipase and amylase—both are normal. Your ultrasound also didn’t show any gallstones or duct blockages. The pancreas that’s left looks normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So if it’s not pancreatitis, what is causing the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the challenge. The pain feels like pancreatitis to you, but the tests don’t confirm it. We’ve also consulted psychiatry to consider whether there might be a component of chronic pain syndrome or conversion disorder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wait—so you’re saying this might be in my head?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at all. Your pain is real. But sometimes, with long-term chronic conditions, the nervous system can become hypersensitive. Psychiatry isn’t saying it’s ‘all in your head’—they’re just helping us look at all possibilities.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess that makes sense. They recommended something about changing my antidepressant?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they suggested possibly switching from amitriptyline to mirtazepine, which might help with both pain and sleep. But we decided to hold off on changing it in the hospital and let your therapist and PMD decide together.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I see. I’ll talk to my therapist about it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s your pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but a little better. I haven’t vomited since yesterday morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’re keeping you NPO for now—no food by mouth—to let your gut rest. You’re getting IV fluids and pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I start eating again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll try small sips of water today. If you tolerate that, we can slowly advance to clear liquids, then a soft diet. But we’ll go step by step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my other meds—can I take them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Once you’re tolerating liquids, we’ll restart your oral meds—like your Protonix for esophagitis, betaxolol and Florinef for your orthostatic hypotension, and your Lexapro.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about methotrexate? I usually take it weekly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held it this week since you’re not eating well. You should discuss with your rheumatologist whether to resume it and if the dose needs adjustment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well overnight—no vomiting, pain is stable. We’re going to try a clear liquid diet this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Can I have apple juice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, small amounts. We’ll watch closely. If you keep it down, we can advance further tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain med? I’m on Dilaudid at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you from IV to oral Dilaudid since you’re starting liquids. Start with 2 mg every 4 hours as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well—you’ve kept down soup and crackers. We’re upgrading you to a regular diet today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news! Does this mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly tomorrow. Your pain is controlled with oral meds, and you’re stable. We just need to finalize your discharge plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about those blood tests? Did they come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most are still pending. The rheumatology team still doesn’t think this is active vasculitis, but you’ll need to follow up with them to review the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my gastroenterologist? I have an appointment tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s perfect. You should definitely keep that. They’ll help coordinate your long-term care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re being discharged today. You’ve tolerated a regular diet, your pain is controlled, and you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What meds should I take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home on your usual meds: betaxolol, Florinef, Protonix, Lexapro, Plaquenil, and amitriptyline at night. For pain, you’ll have Dilaudid 2 mg as needed, and for nausea, Zofran or Compazine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And methotrexate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hold off until you speak with your rheumatologist. They’ll decide if you should restart it based on your symptoms and the pending blood work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any other follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—see your gastroenterologist today, your rheumatologist soon, and your therapist to discuss your medications. And call us or come back if the pain returns and you can’t keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we hope this flare doesn’t come back.
